planting.note: Drill into a firm, well-drained seedbed at 12-15 lb/acre in early spring or late summer; as a soil-building rotation crop, hay or graze before bud stage and plan on three to five productive years before renovating the stand.

directions: Ranger was released by the Nebraska Agricultural Experiment Station and USDA in the early 1940s as a bacterial-wilt-resistant, broadly winter-hardy alfalfa for the central and northern Great Plains. Its deep taproot fixes substantial atmospheric nitrogen and improves soil structure over a multi-year stand, making it a durable choice in longer crop rotations rather than a quick single-season cover. Mow or graze before flowering to maintain forage quality, and terminate the stand by tillage once the fertility-building or forage goals for that rotation cycle are met.

planting.note: Broadcast at 15-20 lb/acre or drill at 10-12 lb/acre on a firm seedbed in spring, or seed in late summer where winters allow full establishment before dormancy.

directions: Vernal was released by the University of Wisconsin in 1953 and became the standard winterhardiness check variety used in alfalfa trials for decades afterward because of its persistence under repeated close cutting and cold-climate stress. As a nitrogen-fixing perennial legume it builds soil fertility and organic matter across a multi-year rotation rather than in a single season. Cut for hay before bloom to preserve quality, or mow and incorporate residue if the stand is being grown primarily as a soil-improving green manure ahead of a demanding row crop.

planting.note: Drill at 10-15 lb/acre into a firm, well-drained seedbed; its deep taproot establishes slowly but tolerates dryland and marginal soils better than most modern cultivars once rooted in.

directions: Ladak was introduced to the United States in the early twentieth century from the Ladakh region of the western Himalayas and became prized for exceptional winter hardiness and drought tolerance on the northern Great Plains. Its slower regrowth after cutting compared to modern cultivars suits it better to occasional hay or soil-building rotations than to intensive multi-cut forage systems. The deep, drought-tolerant taproot makes it a strong nitrogen-fixing option for marginal or dryland fields where fertility building matters more than yield speed, and it was historically used as parent stock in breeding later hardy alfalfa releases.

planting.note: Drill or broadcast at 12-15 lb/acre in spring on well-drained ground; allow a full season of establishment before the first hay or grazing cut in cold-winter regions.

directions: Grimm traces back to seed brought from Franconia, Germany, to Carver County, Minnesota, by immigrant Wendelin Grimm in 1857, where decades of natural winter selection produced the first truly winter-hardy alfalfa for the northern United States. It later served as foundational breeding stock for many of the hardy cultivars that followed it. As a deep-rooted perennial legume it draws up subsoil minerals and fixes nitrogen over a multi-year stand, making it well suited to long rotations aimed at rebuilding soil fertility. Mow before bloom for hay quality, or simply let a stand stand two or more seasons as a fertility-building perennial cover before renovating.

planting.note: Drill at 8-12 lb/acre in spring; give the creeping root system a full year to spread laterally before grazing or haying so the sod-forming stand fills in evenly.

directions: Rambler was developed at the Agriculture Canada research station in Saskatoon and released in the 1950s as a creeping-rooted alfalfa whose lateral roots let it spread and thicken into a dense, sod-like stand rather than growing as isolated crowns. That spreading habit, combined with outstanding winter hardiness and drought tolerance, makes it valuable for long-term pasture and erosion control on the northern Great Plains and Canadian Prairies. As a nitrogen-fixing perennial it steadily improves soil fertility under grazing, and because it tolerates closer, more frequent defoliation than crown-type alfalfas it holds up well in rotational grazing systems used for soil building.
